covers.quote: Use initial capitals for commercial terms
An exception to using initial capitals is where the business itself uses an unusual mix of spacing, capitals and lower case letters. In this case, write it the way the business writes it.
Don’t use an initial capital at the start of sentences when the trade mark or brand starts with a lower case letter.
Use initial capitals for the proprietary names of drugs and other chemicals, but lower case for generic names.
and use a capital letter.
A few words have different meanings when used as a trade mark or used generically.

Other brand names have become so widely used that they are no longer associated with a specific product. They have become common household names used in a generic sense. They start with lower case except at the start of a sentence.

parts.quote: eBay is a popular online auction site.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for trade marks, brands and business names.
rules.violation_condition: A commercial term has casing inconsistent with its proprietary or generic use, or a business’s unconventional name is written with different casing or spacing from the business’s own form. This includes capitalizing a deliberately lower-case brand initial at the start of a sentence.
when: Trade marks, brands, business names and proprietary names of drugs or other chemicals normally take initial capitals.
Preserve a business’s unconventional spacing and capitalization instead of imposing the normal initial-capital pattern.
Preserve a trade mark’s or brand’s lower-case initial even at the start of a sentence.
Generic names of drugs and chemicals use lower case, subject to ordinary sentence-initial capitalization.
Former brand names used as common generic terms use lower case except at the start of a sentence.
Where a word has distinct proprietary and generic senses, its styling depends on the sense used.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates proprietary and generic status, business-specific styling and sentence position as cases of one capitalization check; G-4 absorbs restatements.

covers.quote: ‘Trade mark’ is spelled as 2 words in the Trade Marks Act 1995.
You should also spell ‘trade mark’ as 2 words when you use it as a verb

parts.quote: The trade mark Vegemite was first registered in 1923.

Register your brand as a trade mark if you don’t want others to use it.

rules.quote: Use this spelling when writing for government, even though most dictionaries prefer ‘trademark’.
rules.violation_condition: The noun or verb ‘trade mark’ is written as a single word or a hyphenated form rather than as two words.
when: Applies when using the noun or verb in government writing.
The two-word spelling also applies to verb uses.
rules.why: G-2 keeps noun and verb uses within one spelling check; G-4 absorbs the repeated instruction about verbs.

parts.quote: Register your brand as a trade mark if you don’t want others to use it.

rules.why: This is a separately flaggable wording preference, not another spelling rule; G-4 keeps the two-word spelling instruction in its own consolidated rule.

covers.quote: Avoid using trade marks and brand names if possible. Instead use a generic word.

rules.quote: Use a common word for a product if you can
rules.specification: Treat a generic replacement as possible when it preserves the intended meaning without losing relevant information about a particular brand. This makes the page’s ‘if you can’ condition explicit rather than imposing an absolute ban.
rules.violation_condition: A trade mark or brand name is used for a product where a generic word would convey the intended meaning without losing relevant brand-specific information.
when: A generic product word can convey the intended meaning without identifying a particular brand.
rules.why: G-4 treats the heading and body as one preference for generic product words over trade marks and brand names.

rules.quote: Avoid using the registered (®) symbol or the trade mark (™) symbol for trade marks if possible.
rules.specification: The page does not define when omitting a symbol is impossible. A checker needs an agreed exception policy before treating every occurrence as a finding.
rules.violation_condition: A trade mark is accompanied by ® or ™ even though the symbol could be omitted.
when: The symbol is being used to mark a trade mark, rather than merely being discussed.
The symbol can be omitted.
rules.why: G-2 keeps both symbols under one avoidable-symbol check; this is distinct from the prohibition on using ® for an unregistered mark.

covers.quote: The registered symbol shows a trade mark is registered.
A business doesn’t have to use the symbol for protecting its intellectual property.
The trade mark symbol can be used with registered and unregistered trade marks. Businesses can use it when they intend to register the term or when registration is pending.

rules.quote: It’s illegal to use it if the trade mark is not registered.
rules.violation_condition: The registered symbol ® is used with a trade mark that is not registered.
when: Applies to the registered symbol ® used with a trade mark.
Registration does not require the business to display ®.
This registration restriction does not apply to ™, which may accompany registered or unregistered marks, including intended or pending registrations.
rules.why: The explicit legal prohibition supports MUST_NOT. G-3 treats optional use and the permissions for ™ as qualifications, not additional rules.

covers.quote: This may vary between different countries.
A few words have different meanings when used as a trade mark or used generically.

rules.quote: If a term is still registered as a trade mark, you should use it only for that brand
rules.specification: Read this as restricting use of a registered product name for other brands or products generically, while allowing the distinct generic senses expressly illustrated later, such as ‘bandaid’ for a makeshift solution and ‘google’ for searching the internet.
rules.violation_condition: A currently registered trade mark is used as the name of another brand’s product or as a generic product name rather than referring to the brand it identifies.
when: The term is still registered as a trade mark in the relevant country.
Registration status and the resulting restriction can differ between countries.
Do not flag the distinct generic meanings that the page presents as correct.
rules.why: G-2 retains registration status and country as conditions. The capitalization clause is consolidated into the capitalization rule under G-4, avoiding a duplicate finding.
